data.title: Initial Level Placement
data.description: A high-level scan to establish your current CEFR baseline (A2-B2). One question per grammar point across three bands.

sections.explain: Use the present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) for an action happening now: 'It is raining'. The present simple 'rains' is for habits, and 'It raining' is missing the verb 'is'.

words.word: Look! It rains outside now.
Look! It is raining outside.
Look! It raining outside.

sections.explain: Long adjectives form the comparative with 'more' + adjective + 'than': 'more interesting than'. We don't add '-er' to long adjectives, and we use 'than', not 'as', in comparatives.

words.word: This book is more interesting as that one.
This book is interestinger than that one.
This book is more interesting than that one.

sections.explain: Use no article (zero article) with uncountable nouns in a general sense: 'Water boils...'. 'The water' means specific water, and 'a water' is wrong because water is uncountable.

words.word: The water boils at 100 degrees.
A water boils at 100 degrees.
Water boils at 100 degrees.

sections.explain: Use the present perfect with 'since' + a start point for an action continuing to now: 'have lived ... since 2015'. Use 'since' (not 'for') with a point in time, and the present simple 'live' can't take 'since' here.

words.word: I live here since 2015.
I have lived here for 2015.
I have lived here since 2015.

sections.explain: The second conditional uses 'if' + past simple, then 'would' + base verb: 'If I had ..., I would ...'. We don't use 'would' in the if-clause.

words.word: If I would have more time, I would learn the piano.
If I had more time, I would learn the piano.
If I have more time, I would learn the piano.

sections.explain: 'Must' expresses a confident deduction and is followed by the base verb, with no 'to' and no '-s': 'she must be asleep'. Modals never take 'to' or a third-person '-s'.

words.word: She isn't answering; she must be asleep.
She isn't answering; she must to be asleep.
She isn't answering; she musts be asleep.

sections.explain: Use 'much' with uncountable nouns like 'sugar': 'much sugar'. 'Many' is for countable plurals, and 'sugar' has no plural '-s' here.

words.word: There isn't many sugar left.
There isn't much sugars left.
There isn't much sugar left.

sections.explain: Use the future perfect ('will have' + past participle) for something completed before a future point: 'will have finished'. 'will have finish' lacks the participle, and 'will had' is not a valid form.

words.word: By next June, I will have finish my degree.
By next June, I will had finished my degree.
By next June, I will have finished my degree.

sections.explain: A mixed conditional links a past condition to a present result: 'If I had studied ..., I would be ... now'. The past perfect shows the past cause; 'would be' shows the present result.

words.word: If I studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
If I had studied medicine, I would have be a doctor now.
If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

sections.explain: In reported questions, use statement word order and no auxiliary 'do/did': 'where I lived'. The direct-question forms 'where did I live' / 'where do I live' are incorrect when reported.

words.word: She asked me where did I live.
She asked me where I lived.
She asked me where do I live.
